For this reason, muscle activity is hampered in Parkinson's disease."},{"label":"C","letter":"C","text":"Explain the structure of 'A'.","marks":3,"answer":"Structure A in the above stem is a muscle tissue. This tissue is capable of contracting and expanding to affect movement. The muscle tissue which is shown in the stem is a striated or voluntary muscle tissue. Voluntary muscles can be contracted or expanded at the will of the animal. They are originated from the mesoderm layer of embryo. The cells of this muscle tissue are tubular, unbranched, and have transverse striations. This muscle has myofibrils with striations. These generally have more than one nucleus. The muscle cells are called myocytes which are covered by a membrane called sarcolemma. This muscle can contract or expand quickly and is also called skeletal muscle. So, from above we can say that the structure 'A' is a skeletal or voluntary or striated muscle."},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"Analyze the role of A and B in human locomotion.","marks":4,"answer":"The structure 'A' is a skeletal muscle and 'B' is a bone. They both play vital roles in locomotion in the human body. The skeletal system gives the structure of our body and the muscle covers it. The voluntary muscles are attached to the bones with the help of tendons. Nerve impulses cause muscles to contract. With the withdrawal of the impulse, the muscle relaxes. In this way, muscle helps in locomotion by stretching and extending limbs. Contraction of the muscle draws a bone away or towards the body, rotating, lifting, positioning of the body, etc. By the nerve impulses, we can bend and extend our arm or leg by the simultaneous contraction and relaxation of agonist and antagonist muscles. So, from the aforesaid discussion, we can say that bones of hands, legs, shoulders and the pectoral girdle and pelvic or hip girdle help in movement. They help in the muscle attachment and thus help us to move our whole body.\n---"}]

Explain.","marks":2,"answer":"Diabetes is a metabolic disorder which cannot be cured. That is why, to control diabetes, a set of rules is maintained. They are known as 3D- discipline, diet, and dose. A diabetic patient should be disciplined in his lifestyle, must take a balanced and low-carb diet and take medicines in proper dosage as prescribed by the physician."},{"label":"C","letter":"C","text":"Compare 'C' with 'D' of the given table.","marks":3,"answer":"'C' and 'D' of the stem are ligament and tendon respectively. A comparative discussion on them is given below:
- Definition: Ligaments connect one bone to another. Tendons connect muscles to bones.
- Formed of: Ligaments are made of both white and yellow fibrous connective tissue. Tendons are made of white fibrous connective tissue.
- Branching of the tissue: Ligaments are branched; tendons are unbranched.
- Nature: Ligaments are elastic and strong; tendons are inelastic and tough.
- Fibres: In ligaments, fibres are compactly packed and not arranged in parallel bundles. In tendons, fibres are present as compact parallel bundles.
- Function: Ligaments stabilize the joints during movement and prevent dislocation by restricting actions. Tendons transmit the force which the muscle exerts."},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"Describe the activities of A, B, C and D in animal movement.","marks":4,"answer":"'A', 'B', 'C' and 'D' mentioned in the stem are bone, muscle, ligament and tendon respectively. Their activities in animal movement are described below: In the musculoskeletal system, the muscular and skeletal systems work together to support and move the body. Bones are connected to other bones and muscle fibers via connective tissue such as tendons and ligaments. The bones provide stability to the body. Muscles keep bones in place and also play a role in the movement of bones. To allow motion, different bones are connected by joints. Cartilage prevents the bone ends from rubbing directly onto each other. Muscles contract to move the bone attached to the joint. The muscular system makes the covering of the structure. Muscles remain attached with bones by a strong elastic part named tendon. Muscle contraction is the result of nerve impulses. With the withdrawal of impulses, the muscle again stretches/extends or relaxes. This contraction and relaxation of muscles, attached with the bones, help in movement. Muscles can pull bones, but they can't push them back to the original position. So, they work in pairs of flexors and extensors. At the end of the skeletal muscle, there are tendons connecting the muscle to the bones. Again, bone joints contain ligaments that stabilize the joints during movement and prevent dislocation by restricting actions outside the normal joint range. So, this is how 'A', 'B', 'C' and 'D' work together in animal movement.
---"}]

There are different types of joints, such as:
- Fixed Joints: These joints are rigid and cannot move, such as the sutures in the skull.
- Slightly Movable Joints: These joints are connected but allow slight movement, enabling the body to bend forward, backward, and sideways, as seen in the vertebral joints.
- Freely Movable Joints: These joints allow easy movement. Ball-and-socket joints and hinge joints are the main types in this category. There are four main blood groups: A, B, AB, and O, classified by the presence or absence of antigens on red blood cells and antibodies in plasma. The rules for blood transfusion are:
- Blood Group A: Antigen A, Antibody b, Can donate to A and AB, Can receive from A and O.
- Blood Group B: Antigen B, Antibody a, Can donate to B and AB, Can receive from B and O.
- Blood Group AB: Antigens A and B, No antibodies, Can donate to AB only (universal recipient), Can receive from all groups.
- Blood Group O: No antigens, Antibodies a and b, Can donate to all groups (universal donor), Can receive from O only.
Before blood transfusion, it is crucial to test for blood type, Rh factor, and the presence of pathogens to ensure compatibility and safety.
---"}]

This is a reflex action that protects the retina from excessive light damage. The role of 'Y' (spinal cord/reflex arc) in this incident: Light stimulus is detected by photoreceptors in the retina. The sensory neurons carry this signal to the brain (not spinal cord for pupillary reflex). This is a cranial reflex mediated by the optic nerve (sensory) and oculomotor nerve (motor)."},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"Write down the structure and activity of the 'X' part of the CNS in human body.","marks":4,"answer":"The 'X' part of the CNS is the brain. Its structure and activity in human body is given below: The brain is the swollen part of the nervous system at the top of the spinal cord, inside the skull. It is covered by three layers of protective membranes called meninges. The brain is the manager of the nervous system and is divided into three parts:
(i) Forebrain or Prosencephalon: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, divided into two hemispheres (right and left) by deep furrows, and connected by the corpus callosum. The right hemisphere controls the left side of the body and the left hemisphere controls the right side. The cerebrum has a folded surface covered by protective meninges. It is responsible for body movement, voluntary muscle control, and conscious activities such as speech, vision, hearing, intelligence, memory, and thinking.
(ii) Midbrain or Mesencephalon: It is the bridge between the forebrain and hindbrain. It helps coordinate muscle activities, maintain balance, and support vision and hearing functions.
(iii) Hindbrain or Rhombencephalon: This consists of cerebellum, pons and medulla oblongata.
- The cerebellum is located behind the pons with an outer grey matter layer and inner white matter. It controls muscle tension, balance, movement coordination, and voluntary muscle activities.
- The pons is situated between the medulla oblongata and midbrain, connecting these regions.
- The medulla oblongata links the pons to the spinal cord and gives rise to 8 of the 12 cranial nerve pairs, controlling the heart, lungs, swallowing, hearing, and balance.
---"}]

These cells are found solitary or in pairs and are densely scattered out within the matrix."},{"label":"C","letter":"C","text":"Explain the different types as indicated.","marks":3,"answer":"The stem indicates different types of joints. They are explained below:
- Synovial joint: When two ends of two bones touches, it makes a joint to form a synovial bone joint. When more than two bones make a joint, it is called complex synovial joint. The parts of synovial joints are: bone ends are covered with cartilage, and synovial fluids and a cover or capsule which is a tough fibrous tissue or ligament that firmly holds the joint.
- Fixed joint: The bones are joined firmly, so it is immoveable. Example - joint of the cranium.
- Slightly movable joint: These joints are joined with one another and has a small sliding surface. So, we can bend the body. Example - joint of back bone.
- Freely movable joint: These joints can be moved easily. Example - wrist joint ball and socket joint.
- Ball and socket joint: Joints where the round one head of the bone fits into a cup shaped socket or cavity of another bone in such a way that it allows the bone's movement in all planes. This is also a type of synovial joints. For example: Shoulder joint, ball and socket joint of thigh bone.
- Hinge joint: The elbows, knees, joints of the finger are the examples of hinge joints. It moves like a hinge of a door. It can be moved in one plane only. These are also examples of synovial joints."},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"Analyze the function of cited frame.","marks":4,"answer":"The cited frame is human skeleton. The functions of human skeleton are given below:
(i) Structure and firmness of the body - The skeleton forms the hard structure of the body and gives a definite shape to the body. It joins lower organs with upper organs.
(ii) Protection - The skull protects the brain, the spinal cord within the vertebral column or backbone, and the lungs and heart within the thorax. Muscles are attached to the skeleton and skeletal muscles are involved in carrying the weight of the body.
(iii) Movement and Locomotion - Hands, legs, shoulders and the pectoral girdle and pelvic or hip girdle help in movement. The Muscular system has an important role in this act. Due to the attachment of muscles with the bones, we can move the bones and our bodies move.
(iv) Production of red blood cells - Bone marrow produces red blood cells.
(v) Storage of mineral salts - Bones store mineral salts (calcium, potassium, phosphorus). This is why the bones remain hard and strong.
---"}]

In this way various muscles help in the movement of different organs.
---"}]

Why is it called complex tissue?","marks":2,"answer":"The tissue made up of more than one type of cells which coordinate together to perform a common function is called a complex tissue. Complex tissue is called vascular tissue because it consists of specialized cells that form a network of vessels for the transport of fluids, water, and nutrients throughout plants. It provides structural support and enable efficient movement of substances in the plant. Vascular tissue includes both xylem, which transports water and minerals, and phloem, which transports sugars and organic compounds."},{"label":"C","letter":"C","text":"Draw a labelled diagram of the figure in the stem.","marks":3,"answer":"[Diagram description: Labeled diagram of a nephron showing glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct.]"},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"Describe the purification process of blood in human.","marks":4,"answer":"Blood purification in humans occurs in the kidneys. The process: Blood enters kidney via renal artery, filtered in glomerulus. Filtrate passes through Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule (reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, salts) → loop of Henle (water and salt balance) → distal tubule (secretion of wastes) → collecting duct (urine formation). Urine passes to ureter → bladder → urethra. Clean blood returns via renal vein.\n---"}]
